destination.title: Police Can Search Your Car Without a Warrant — Except One Place

short32: The police can search your car without a warrant — and they have for a hundred years.
But there's one place they still can't follow it.
It goes back to 1925 and a Prohibition bootlegger named Carroll.
Agents tore open his seats and found sixty-eight bottles of whisky — no warrant.
The Court said a car isn't a house: it can be driven off before a warrant is ever signed.
So with probable cause, police can search it on the spot.
But probable cause is the catch.
Being pulled over isn't permission, and a hunch isn't enough — an officer needs a real, specific reason.
And the search only reaches where the thing they're after could fit.
Chasing a stolen television doesn't let them open a pill bottle.
An officer walked up a driveway, lifted a tarp off a motorcycle he believed was stolen, and confirmed it.
In 2018, by eight to one, the Supreme Court said no.
The driveway hugging your home is curtilage — part of the house — and the car-search power stops there.
It extends, the Court said, no further than the car itself.
Watch the full story on the channel.

candidate_payload_lines: Chief Justice Taft wrote that you can't treat the two the same, "because the vehicle can be quickly moved out of the locality or jurisdiction in which the warrant must be sought." So the Court carved out what we now call the **automobile exception**.
Justice Sotomayor, writing for the Court, said it in one line worth keeping: "The scope of the automobile exception extends no further than the automobile itself." So both things are true at once.
The police can search your car without a warrant.
Because there is one place they still can't go — and in 2018 the Supreme Court drew that line at the very edge of your home.
And it hasn't since 1925 — a hundred years ago.
Carroll's lawyers had what sounds like a winning argument: no warrant, no search.
If police have probable cause to believe your car contains contraband, they can search it — right there, no warrant.
That 1925 rule is still the rule behind why an ordinary traffic stop can, under the right facts, become an open trunk on the shoulder of the highway.
Acevedo in 1991 — which held that a closed bag or a locked box inside the car gets no special shield of its own.
In 2018, by a vote of eight to one, the Court held that the car-search power does not reach onto the ground that belongs to your home.
So here's the actual map of your rights on the road — the one almost nobody is handed.
On a public street or a routine stop, your car can be searched without a warrant — but only with probable cause, and only as far as the thing they're looking for could actually be.
But the Supreme Court has never set a single nationwide rule on that — and in states that have legalized or decriminalized it, several courts now say the odor by itself isn't enough anymore.
If you drive, that line is yours — and most people go their whole lives never knowing exactly where it falls.
era_note: Two eras in one episode. The 1925 Carroll origin is Prohibition-era America; probable cause, the scope rule, arrest, rentals and the marijuana-odor question are present day. Each Short declares its own era token and keeps its generated plates inside it; modern stock footage is only bound to the present-day Short.

shorts.angle: The automobile exception no longer requires any emergency at all: the Court has held that a drivable car plus probable cause is enough, with no ticking clock and no proof anyone was about to leave.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: If the car being a car is emergency enough, is there any ground left where that power finally stops?
shorts.loop_join: L8 states that the emergency the rule was built on stopped being required long ago, which is exactly the finding L1 opens with — a search that needs no emergency at all.

lines.text: The Supreme Court has said police need no emergency to search your car. The car being a car is the emergency.
source_lines: They don't even have to prove a separate emergency, though.

The Justices spelled that out again in the nineteen-nineties: a car that's readily mobile, plus probable cause, needs nothing more. No ticking clock. No proof the driver was about to speed off. The car being a car is the emergency.

lines.text: The rule was written in 1925 for a reason. A house stays put. Officers can post someone at the door and wait.
source_lines: A house, the Court said, stays put.
If officers have to leave and get a warrant, they can post someone at the door; the house isn't going anywhere.

lines.text: A car is built to move. Taft wrote that a vehicle can be moved out of the jurisdiction where a warrant is sought.
source_lines: But a car is built to move.
Chief Justice Taft wrote that you can't treat the two the same, "because the vehicle can be quickly moved out of the locality or jurisdiction in which the warrant must be sought."

lines.text: The Court did not stop at the runaway car. In the nineteen-nineties it said a drivable car and probable cause need nothing more.
source_lines: The Court has been blunt about it: if the car is drivable and there's probable cause, that's enough — no extra excuse required.

lines.text: No ticking clock. No proof the driver was about to speed off. The reason for the exception need not be present.
source_lines: No ticking clock. No proof the driver was about to speed off.

lines.text: Not everyone agreed in 1925. Justice McReynolds, joined by Justice Sutherland, dissented. They lost, and the exception has governed your glovebox since.
source_lines: Not everyone agreed at the time. Justice McReynolds, joined by Justice Sutherland, dissented.
And the Court gave an answer that has governed your glovebox ever since.

lines.text: Your car holds your bag, your phone, your paperwork. It carries thinner protection than your living room, for a reason written in 1925.
source_lines: Your car is where you keep your bag, your phone, your paperwork, half of your private life while it's in motion.
And it carries far thinner protection than your living room — for a reason written down before your grandparents were born.

lines.text: The emergency that justified the rule stopped being required long ago. It is enough now that the car could, in theory, drive away.
source_lines: The Court has been blunt about it: if the car is drivable and there's probable cause, that's enough — no extra excuse required.

shorts.avoids: Short 32 told the Carroll story, probable cause and the driveway line; this cut is the one element it never touched — that the urgency justifying the rule no longer has to exist.

shorts.angle: Three limits on the car-search power that sit on the public road itself: an arrest does not open the car, a rental driver keeps privacy, and the marijuana odor question has never been settled nationwide.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: Which of these limits an officer actually has to respect at your own window, and where the car-search power finally runs out of road.
shorts.loop_join: L8 says the exception is not infinite and an arrest does not widen it, handing straight back to L1's flat statement that being arrested does not open your car.

lines.text: Being arrested does not open your car. Once you are handcuffed and away from it, officers generally cannot search it for that alone.
source_lines: Being arrested doesn't automatically open the car either. In a case called Gant, the Court said that once you're handcuffed and set away from the vehicle, officers generally can't search it just because they arrested you — not unless it's reasonable to think evidence of that specific offense is inside.

lines.text: That rule came from a case called Gant. What is left is narrow: evidence of the specific offense they arrested you for.
source_lines: Being arrested doesn't automatically open the car either. In a case called Gant, the Court said that once you're handcuffed and set away from the vehicle, officers generally can't search it just because they arrested you — not unless it's reasonable to think evidence of that specific offense is inside.

lines.text: The protection can follow you into a rental car. The Court has said a lawful driver keeps a real expectation of privacy.
source_lines: The protection can even follow you into a rental. The Court has said that if you're lawfully driving a rental car, you can keep a real expectation of privacy in it — even if your name isn't on the paperwork.

lines.text: Even if your name is not on the paperwork. That undoes what most drivers assume about a car they did not rent.
source_lines: The protection can even follow you into a rental. The Court has said that if you're lawfully driving a rental car, you can keep a real expectation of privacy in it — even if your name isn't on the paperwork.

lines.text: Then there is one honest gray area. For years, in many places, the smell of marijuana alone was treated as probable cause.
source_lines: And there's one honest gray area worth naming. For years, in many places, the smell of marijuana alone was treated as probable cause.

lines.text: The Supreme Court has never set a nationwide rule on that. Courts in states that legalized it now say odor is not enough.
source_lines: But the Supreme Court has never set a single nationwide rule on that — and in states that have legalized or decriminalized it, several courts now say the odor by itself isn't enough anymore.

lines.text: So the honest answer is that it depends where you are. The same smell at the same window means different things elsewhere.
source_lines: On that one, the honest answer is: it depends where you are.

lines.text: The exception is broader than most believe. It is not a myth. It is just not infinite, and an arrest does not widen it.
source_lines: The exception is broad — broader than most people believe — and it isn't a myth. It's just not infinite.
